terms.grammar: noun, fifth declension, with an adjective
evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.39: rēs pūblica rēs populī
terms.comment: Classically the state, whatever its constitution: for Cicero a kingdom is a rēs pūblica too (Rep. 1.42). It means a republic where the context sets it against kings, as Levi and Bini allow (p. 54), and in the names of states: annō sextō Reī Pūblicae Gallicae, in the sixth year of the French Republic (Desfontaines, 1798, in Morgan–Owens).

terms.gloss: liberty: a state free of kings
evidence: Tac. Ann. 1.1: lībertātem et cōnsulātum L. Brūtus īnstituit
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: the political freedom of a people not under monarchical rule. To the Romans the end of the kings was the beginning of liberty.

terms.gloss: a republic, a state of the people
terms.grammar: noun phrase: rēs pūblica with the adjective populāris
terms.comment: Levi and Bini’s phrase, with populāre imperium, for a republic as against a kingdom.

phrases.latin: līberī jam hinc populī Rōmānī rēs pāce bellōque gestās, annuōs magistrātūs, imperiaque lēgum potentiōra quam hominum peragam
phrases.english: from here on I shall tell the deeds of the Roman people, now free, in peace and war: their magistrates elected for a year, and the rule of laws stronger than the rule of men
